All esophageal foreign bodies require immediate evaluation for possible endoscopic removal. C

background.definition: A gastrointestinal foreign body is any object that has the potential to cause gastrointestinal obstructive complications such as aspiration, bowel obstruction, or perforation.

list.listitem: Most foreign body ingestions occur in children.
The next most common patients with foreign body ingestions are edentulous adults, prisoners, and patients with psychiatric disease.
About 1500 deaths from foreign body ingestion in the United States annually.
In children, some of the most common causes of GI foreign bodies are coins, food and bones, pins, fidget spinners, and batteries (especially lithium ion button batteries).
In adults, some of the most common causes of GI foreign bodies are food and bones, fiber products, pills, and coins.

A systematic review of upper GI tract foreign body in adults found that fish bones were most common and esophagus the most common location. Complications occurred in 4% and patients were divided evenly between men and women.
A systematic review found that rectal foreign bodies are mostly self-inserted sexual devices (36%) and glass objects (18%), and occur in a male to female ratio of 6:1.
Esophageal obstruction due to a coin is usually not associated with esophageal abnormalities.
Esophageal obstruction due to meat or food can be associated with anatomical abnormalities, esophageal cancer or mucosal abnormalities (such as eosinophilic esophagitis).
Pointed objects in the esophagus (pins, nails, razors) are associated with a high risk of esophageal perforation.
Disc batteries will lead to a significant esophageal burn quickly due to their alkaline electrolytes.
If more than one magnet is ingested, a patient is at high risk of intestinal perforation and volvulus due to magnetic attraction across loops of bowel within the GI tract.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Size of child (6 months-6 years old)

list.listitem: Symptoms vary by location of the foreign body. C
Chest and abdominal radiographs are important to determine the presence of a foreign body and to determine its clearance. C
Food impaction in children may be associated with eosinophilic esophagitis. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Chest pain, “burning” sensation, abdominal pain, feeding problem in infants
History of atopy, feeding problem as infant, history of recurrent food impaction
History of psychiatric disease (eg, hair or trichobezoar)

list.listitem: A history and physical examination are very helpful in determining the general location of a symptomatic foreign body. The physician should try to determine the type and number of foreign bodies ingested by history.
Patients presenting with dysphagia, odynophagia, excessive drooling, or respiratory distress typically will have an esophageal foreign body.

The clinical presentation depends on location.
Esophagus: choking or gagging (49%), vomiting (47%), dysphagia (42%), drooling, feeding problems, throat/chest pain, upper respiratory symptoms if tracheal compression. A systematic review found that the most common symptoms were retrosternal pain (78%), dysphagia (48% and odynophagia (43%). Stomach: Abdominal pain, symptoms of gastric outlet obstruction (rare). Intestinal: Abdominal pain, symptoms of obstruction (rare).

A complete abdominal examination, including assessing for bowel sounds, determining location of tenderness, and determining rebound and guarding will help in deciding if a gastric or intestinal foreign body is causing obstruction or perforation. However in a large retrospective cohort, most patients were symptomatic but had normal physical exams.

A retrospective review of 73 children presenting to a pediatric tertiary care center for coin ingestion revealed that 68 children (93%) had symptoms of drooling, pain, or sensation of object; 5 children (7%) had no symptoms.

A larger retrospective series of 543 children with suspected foreign body who underwent esophagoscopy found that the most common symptoms were choking or gagging, vomiting, and dysphagia/odynophagia; each were present in just under half of children.

Chest radiographs should be obtained for any child with a history of foreign body ingestion as esophageal foreign bodies can be asymptomatic. However, it is important to note that in a series of 543 children with suspected foreign body ingestion, 59% with a foreign body had a normal CXR.

Abdominal radiographs should be followed serially to show that the foreign body has cleared the stomach and intestine. If the swallowed object is not radio-opaque, order a upper GI barium study or esophagoscopy. Consider CT of abdomen/chest if clinically indicated (failure to localize object by other means but high index of suspicion or signs of complications such as perforation or obstruction).

Plain lateral radiographs of the neck are 92% sensitive and 80% specific for detection of cervical esophageal foreign body compared to esophagoscopy as the reference standard in a series of 290 patients, all of whom underwent esophagoscopy.

Esophagoscopy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the reference standard test. It should be considered for any patient with suspected foreign body when radiographs are abnormal or the index of suspicion is high even in the presence of normal radiographs. While flexible endoscopy is the usual standard, a systematic review argued for a continued role of rigid endoscopy under anesthesia in selected patients.

After a careful history and physical examination, obtain chest and/or abdominal radiographs to locate object. However, a normal CXR does not rule out an esophageal foreign body . Evaluate object by radiograph carefully. A “double disc sign” of a circular radio-opaque object indicates a disc battery and not a coin.
If the swallowed object is not radio-opaque, order a upper GI barium study. Consider CT of abdomen if clinically indicated.
Flexible esophageal endoscopy is usually the most essential tool for diagnosis and treatment.

Intervals for radiography are as follows: long and short blunt object > weekly radiograph; coins > weekly radiographs; sharp and pointed objects > daily radiograph once past duodenum; magnets > serial radiographs if continues to move and patient is asymptomatic; disk batteries > radiographs ever 3 to 4 days.
All esophageal foreign bodies should be removed within 24 hours. B
Gastric and intestinal foreign bodies usually require observation and serial abdominal radiographs. C
Esophageal button batteries require immediate endoscopic removal. B
If more than one magnet is ingested, immediate surgical consultation is required. B

A systematic review identified 5 randomized trials with 1185 subjects comparing glucagon with a placebo or another therapy. They found that glucagon had no effect on treatment success (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 - 1.17) but did cause adverse events (mostly vomiting) in 15% compared with none in placebo groups.
Therapy depends on the object ingested. A systematic review of 7 observational studies reported that the most common esophageal FB was fishbones.

A cap-assisted endoscopic technique for removal of impacted esophageal foreign bodies was more likely to be effective than a conventional approach. This technique involves using a transparent cap, usually used for endoscopic mucosal resection, which is placed on the tip of the endoscope and allows for retrieval using continuous suction.
Glucagon 1 mg IV is no more effective than placebo in facilitating removing of an esophageal foreign body.

Coins in the esophagus require endoscopic removal within 24 hours or sooner if significant airway or upper GI tract compromise is present. Coins in the stomach or intestine can be observed by serial radiographs, and if no passage occurs after 12 to 24 hours in the esophagus or 3 to 4 weeks in the stomach, endoscopic or surgical removal may be necessary.

Esophageal coins have been removed by other means (Foley catheter extraction or bougienage); however, there is the risk of aspiration or perforation from pushing against a distal obstruction (peptic stricture, etc.). Asymptomatic esophageal coins can be observed safety for 24 hours as they may pass spontaneously.
Narcotic packets should not be removed endoscopically if this may result in rupture or leakage. They should be removed surgically if they fail to progress or if obstruction occurs.

Food impactions can be removed endoscopically by (1) piecemeal removal through the mouth or (2) pushing food into the stomach with a scope. Evaluate the esophageal mucosa for eosinophilic esophagitis and consider upper GI barium series to rule out an anatomical esophageal abnormality.

All batteries in the esophagus need immediate endoscopic removal. Disk (lithium ion button) batteries in the esophagus should be removed endoscopically, and surgical removal should be considered if they do not make progress through the bowels.
Serious potential compications of esophageal button batteries include aorto-esophageal fistulas, tracheoesophageal fistulae and vocal cord paralysis.
Batteries in the stomach or intestine usually do not require removal (unless there is abdominal pain) but require serial radiographs to document passage.

If more than one magnet is ingested, surgical consultation is mandatory due to risk of volvulus and perforation due to magnetic attraction. Magnets within reach are an indication for urgent endoscopy. If the magnet does not move through the GI tract, surgical removal should be considered.
A retrospective cohort of 596 pediatric high-powered magnets ingestions found that 46% required endoscopy and 55% hospitalization, although there were no reported deaths.

Sharp objects in the esophagus (pin, nail, razor, etc.) need immediate endoscopic (with overtube) or surgical removal. Most sharp objects in the stomach or intestine pass without complications and do not need intervention unless there is associated pain or they fail to progress for 3 days in a row. Serial abdominal radiographs are mandatory.

Rarely, a sharp foreign body such as a fish bone can result in esophageal perforation and medistinal abscess. This usually requires surgical intervention. A case report described use of video-mediastinoscopy to remove two fish bones.
For patients with esophageal perforation or when the esophageal FB is endoscopically unretrievable, surgery is necessary.
Removal of rectal foreign bodies required general anesthesia in 45% of patients and sedation in 29% in a systematic review.
Do not use meat tenderizer to treat an esophageal food impaction.
Hospitalize patients with significant airway or upper GI obstruction and consult gastroenterology or surgery.
Hospitalize patients with a foreign body in the stomach or intestine who have significant abdominal pain and consult surgery.
Most patients do very well clinically after foreign body removal. B
In one series successful removal of lithium ion button batteries was 95% on the first attempt, followed by a course of corticosteroids and then successful removal on the second attempt. B

Esophageal perforations have a poorer outcome with an 11.9% overall mortality rate and a mean length of stay of 32.9 day. However, the mortality rate of perforations associated with a foreign body was only 2.1% in one systematic review.
Aortoesophageal fistula is the most common cause of death following ingestion of a button battery. B
Parents should check the floor and low-lying places in their homes and remove items that could be ingested by children.
If a child ingests an obstructing foreign body, parents should be clear about the type of object ingested.
